import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 868

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/868](https://www.erdosproblems.com/868)
- [LaLa26] Larsen and Larsen, [Erdős problem 868](https://github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-868/blob/main/868.pdf) (2026)
-/

open Filter

open scoped Pointwise

namespace Erdos868

/-- The number of ways in which a natural `n` can be written as the sum of
`o` members of the set `A`. -/
noncomputable
def ncard_add_repr (A : Set ℕ) (o : ℕ) (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  { a : Fin o → ℕ | Set.range a ⊆ A ∧ ∑ i, a i = n }.ncard

/-- Let $A$ be an additive basis of order $2$, let $f(n)$ denote the number of ways in which
$n$ can be written as the sum of two elements from $A$. If $f(n) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$, then
must $A$ contain a minimal additive basis of order $2$?

Larsen and Larsen [LaLa26] answered this in the negative.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_868.parts.i :
    answer(False) ↔ ∀ (A : Set ℕ), A.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 →
      atTop.Tendsto (fun n => ncard_add_repr A 2 n) atTop → ∃ B ⊆ A,
      B.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 ∧ ∀ b ∈ B, ¬(B \ {b}).IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 := by
  sorry

/-- Let $A$ be an additive basis of order $2$, let $f(n)$ denote the number of ways in which
$n$ can be written as the sum of two elements from $A$. If $f(n) > \epsilon \log n$ for large $n$
and an arbitrary fixed $\epsilon > 0$, then must $A$ contain a minimal additive
basis of order $2$?

Larsen and Larsen [LaLa26] constructed a counterexample with $f(n) > c \log n$ for all large $n$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_868.parts.ii :
    answer(False) ↔ ∀ᵉ (A : Set ℕ) (ε > 0), A.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 →
      (∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in atTop, ε * Real.log n < ncard_add_repr A 2 n) → ∃ B ⊆ A,
      B.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 ∧ ∀ b ∈ B, ¬(B \ {b}).IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 := by
  sorry

/-- Erdős and Nathanson proved that this is true if $f(n) > (\log \frac{4}{3})^{-1} \log n$ for
all large $n$. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_868.variants.fixed_ε :
    answer(True) ↔ ∀ (A : Set ℕ), A.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 →
      (∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in atTop, (Real.log (4 / 3))⁻¹ * Real.log n < ncard_add_repr A 2 n) → ∃ B ⊆ A,
      B.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 ∧ ∀ b ∈ B, ¬(B \ {b}).IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 := by
  sorry

/-- Härtter and Nathanson proved that there exist additive bases which do not contain
any minimal additive bases. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11,
  formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
    "https://github.com/hjyuh/formal-conjectures/blob/e0da6ec78953b17618895a093d4bee90fd3f6f67/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/868.lean#L132"]
theorem erdos_868.variants.Hartter_Nathanson (o : ℕ) (ho : 1 < o) : ∃ (A : Set ℕ),
    A.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder o ∧ ∀ B ⊆ A, B.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder o →
    ∃ b ∈ B, (B \ {b}).IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder o := by
  sorry

end Erdos868

findings.description: The quantitative hypothesis matches the current Erdős Problems webpage, but conflicts with the primary theorem and the cited Larsen–Larsen paper. Write C = 1/log(4/3). Lean assumes the ordered representation count R(n) = ncard_add_repr A 2 n exceeds C log n eventually. Erdős–Nathanson instead assume that the unordered count r(n) exceeds c log n eventually for some fixed c > C. Since R(n) = 2r(n) − δ(n), with δ(n) ∈ {0,1}, their hypothesis is equivalent to an eventual ordered-count bound with some coefficient strictly greater than 2C. The file thus both loses the normalization factor and omits the strictly larger fixed coefficient. This is flagged as questionable, rather than a definite misformalization, because the webpage explicitly states the same stronger formula as Lean; the cited sources need reconciliation.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős–Nathanson, Systems of distinct representatives and minimal bases in additive number theory (1979), pp. 89, 97 and Theorem 2 on p. 100, https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1979-25.pdf: r counts representations with a_j ≤ a_k, and the theorem requires “r(n) > c log n for some constant c > log⁻¹(4/3).” Larsen–Larsen, §1, https://github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-868/blob/main/868.pdf, explicitly defines r_A using a ≤ b and repeats this condition. In contrast, https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/868 explicitly gives 1_A*1_A(n) > (log(4/3))⁻¹ log n.
findings.suggested_fix: If this variant is intended to record the Erdős–Nathanson theorem, retain the ordered counter but replace its growth hypothesis by `∃ c : ℝ, 2 * (Real.log (4 / 3))⁻¹ < c ∧ ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in atTop, c * Real.log n < ncard_add_repr A 2 n`. Alternatively use an unordered counter and quantify a coefficient strictly greater than `(Real.log (4 / 3))⁻¹`. Update the docstring accordingly. If retaining the webpage's stronger threshold, supply a reference establishing that version.

reformulations.difference: Lean counts ordered tuples, matching the website's convolution, whereas the cited Larsen–Larsen paper counts unordered pairs.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For each A and n, the unordered count r and Lean's ordered count R satisfy r ≤ R ≤ 2r. Consequently R(n) tends to infinity exactly when r(n) does. The counting convention therefore does not change this question or its negative answer.

reformulations.difference: Lean uses ordered representations and records the negative answer as `False ↔` a universally quantified implication; Larsen–Larsen state an existential counterexample using unordered representations.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Negating the universal implication gives a basis A and ε > 0 with the eventual logarithmic lower bound and no minimal subbasis. The existence of such a positive logarithmic lower bound is invariant under changing counts: r ≤ R transfers a bound from r to R, while R ≤ 2r transfers a bound with coefficient ε for R to one with coefficient ε/2 for r. No prescribed numerical coefficient is being preserved in this part.

reformulations.difference: The absence of a minimal subbasis is expressed by saying every subbasis has a removable element, rather than by explicitly forbidding minimal proper-subset bases.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a fixed order, the basis property is upward closed under inclusion. If a proper subset C of B is a basis, choose b ∈ B \ C; then C ⊆ B \ {b}, so deleting b preserves the basis property. Conversely, deleting an element gives a proper subset. Classical negation then identifies the Lean condition with the absence of any minimal subbasis. Both equivalences were proved in the scratch file.

could_not_verify: Erdos868.erdos_868.variants.fixed_ε: the stronger threshold stated by the webpage and Lean could not be confirmed from the primary references, which require a differently normalized bound with a strictly larger fixed coefficient.
review.notes: All five declarations were reviewed. The website and Larsen–Larsen agree with the two negative answers and solved status. The general-order Härtter–Nathanson statement is supported by the 1987 survey's example {1} ∪ hℕ. The external formal-conjectures proof link was not opened, respecting the repository-consultation restriction. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles without errors: it proves representation-set finiteness, checks empty and order-zero cases, connects the counter to a computable finite enumeration, proves R_univ(n)=n+1 and satisfiability of all growth hypotheses, and proves the minimality equivalences. The reciprocal and division are real-valued; log at zero is irrelevant to the eventual conditions. No definite defect was found against the current webpage; the reported concern is the conflicting quantitative theorem in the primary literature.
